blocks.text: How to Set Up Claude Code (2026 Step-by-Step Guide)
Claude Code installs in under a minute, but a real setup, CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, sub-agents, hooks, permissions, is what makes it useful past day one.

Updated October 2026. Install, auth and settings commands re-checked against Anthropic's Claude Code docs on October 24, 2026.

Claude Code shipped as a research preview in early 2025 and became Anthropic's flagship terminal agent through 2026. By now most engineering teams are no longer asking whether to try it. They are asking how to install it correctly, plug it into the rest of their stack, and avoid the rough edges that come with a tool moving this fast.
Quick setup (3 steps):

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash on macOS, Linux and WSL, or irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex in Windows PowerShell (Homebrew: brew install --cask claude-code; WinGet: winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode)
Run claude and follow the browser prompts to log in
Run claude again from your repo root
That gets you a working session. Everything below walks through the full setup end-to-end so you keep it working.

The install command itself is one line. The interesting part is everything after: picking an auth method, writing a CLAUDE.md the agent will actually respect, wiring up MCP servers without leaking credentials, adding sub-agents that stay in scope, and locking down permissions so the agent does not run rm -rf on a tired Friday. None of that is hard, but skipping it is the difference between a tool that helps and a tool that gets uninstalled in a week.

This guide walks through the full 2026 setup end-to-end. Prerequisites, install, auth, first-run configuration, CLAUDE.md template, MCP servers, sub-agents, hooks, permissions, and a sanity test. Copy-paste commands throughout, with notes for macOS, Linux, and Windows (WSL). By the end you will have a working ~/.claude/ and a project-level .claude/ that you can commit to git.
Prerequisites
Before installing, confirm the basics. Claude Code is a Node-based CLI that talks to Anthropic's API (or an enterprise cloud provider), so you need a terminal, a runtime, and a credential.
A modern terminal. macOS Terminal, iTerm2, Warp, Ghostty, Alacritty, WezTerm, Windows Terminal, or anything that supports ANSI colors and Unicode. Avoid the legacy Windows console host.
Node.js only for the npm route. The native installer needs no Node. If you choose npm, the docs list Node.js 22 or newer. Verify with node --version.
An Anthropic API key or a Claude Pro/Max subscription or an AWS Bedrock / Google Vertex setup with Claude models enabled. Pick one, you do not need all three.
Git. Not strictly required, but Claude Code is dramatically more useful in a git repo because it reads diffs, branches, and history natively.
Roughly 200 MB of disk. The CLI plus its cache fits in well under that on a fresh install.

On Windows, install through WSL2 (Ubuntu or Debian). Native Windows install works for casual use but breaks subtly around shell hooks, file watchers, and MCP servers that expect POSIX paths. WSL is the supported path in 2026.
Step 1: Install
Anthropic's setup docs recommend the native installer. It ships a self-contained binary that updates itself in the background:

On Windows PowerShell, use irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex. In Windows CMD, use curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd. You do not need to run either as Administrator.
Confirm it landed:
You should see a version number. If claude is not found, the install directory is not on your PATH yet. Open a new terminal window first, then check that ~/.local/bin is on your PATH.
Alternative: npm. Anthropic still supports a global npm install, which pulls the same native binary. The docs list Node.js 22 or newer for the npm package:
Do not use sudo with it. If claude is not found afterward, add $(npm prefix -g)/bin to your shell rc file and reopen the terminal.

Alternative: Homebrew or WinGet. Anthropic's docs list two Homebrew casks: brew install --cask claude-code follows the stable channel (typically about a week behind, skipping releases with major regressions) and claude-code@latest gets new versions as soon as they ship. On Windows, winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode works too. Neither Homebrew nor WinGet installs auto-update: run brew upgrade claude-code or winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode yourself.

Alternative: Docker. Anthropic publishes anthropic/claude-code images. Useful for sandboxed agents and CI jobs where you do not want the CLI touching the host. Mount your repo in as a volume and pass the API key via env var.
Pick one install method and stick with it. Mixing npm-global and brew installs causes PATH confusion that wastes an afternoon to debug.
Step 2: Authenticate
Claude Code supports three auth modes in 2026. Pick the one that matches how you already pay for Claude.

Option A: Anthropic API key (most common for individual devs). Generate a key at console.anthropic.com -> Settings -> API Keys. Then either set the env var below (Claude Code asks you to approve the key the first time it sees it) or choose the Anthropic Console account at the /login prompt:
Put that line in ~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, or a per-project .envrc if you use direnv. The CLI reads it on every launch.

Option B: Claude Pro / Max subscription. If you already pay for Claude.ai personally, you can sign in with the same account and your Claude Code usage counts against your subscription's message limits instead of metered API billing. Run claude and follow the browser prompts, or sign in from your shell before the first session:

It opens a browser for OAuth. Inside a session, /login and /logout switch accounts. This is the cheapest path for solo developers (Pro is $20/month, or $17/month billed annually, on claude.com/pricing; heavy API users can spend far more).
Option C: AWS Bedrock or Google Vertex. For teams with existing cloud contracts, data-residency requirements, or VPC-only policies. Set:
Your normal AWS / GCP credentials (via aws configure or gcloud auth) are picked up automatically. Billing flows through your cloud account, not Anthropic.
Test the auth by running claude in any directory. If you see the prompt and can type a message, you are in.
Step 3: First-run config
On first launch Claude Code creates ~/.claude/ and walks you through a short config wizard. Most defaults are fine, but a few are worth setting deliberately.

Working directory. The agent operates inside the directory you launched it from. Always launch from your repo root, not your home directory. Running claude at ~ gives the agent access to dotfiles, SSH keys, and browser profiles. Don't.

Default model. Use the aliases rather than version numbers: opus (latest Opus, Claude Opus 5.5 as of October 2026), sonnet (Sonnet 5.5), haiku (Haiku 5.5) and fable for the hardest, longest tasks (Fable 5.1; on subscriptions Claude Code asks before a Fable request bills usage credits). If you set nothing, Claude Code uses your account's default model. Switch mid-session with /model.
Theme. Dark, light, or auto. Cosmetic only.

Telemetry. Usage metrics and error reports are not a settings key. To turn them off, set DISABLE_TELEMETRY and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING to "1" in the env block of settings.json (or in your shell), or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC to cut all non-essential traffic.
Editor. The CLI shells out to your $EDITOR for multi-line input. Set export EDITOR=nvim (or code -w, or whatever you use) in your shell rc.
Config lives at ~/.claude/settings.json. You can edit it directly:
autoUpdatesChannel takes "latest" (new versions as they ship) or "stable" (a delayed, safer schedule).
For a project-level override, create .claude/settings.json in your repo. Project settings beat user settings. Commit this file: it is how your team shares the same defaults.
Step 4: Write your first CLAUDE.md

CLAUDE.md is the single most important file in your setup. It is the project memory the agent reads at the start of every session. A good CLAUDE.md cuts your token usage in half and stops the agent from re-discovering your stack on every turn.

Step 5: Add an MCP server

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how Claude Code talks to external systems: filesystems, databases, APIs, browsers, design tools. By 2026 there are hundreds of MCP servers, but the canonical "hello world" is the filesystem server.
Install the filesystem MCP server:

That registers a server named filesystem that gives the agent read/write access to /Users/you/projects. Restart claude and run /mcp. You should see filesystem listed as connected, with tools like read_file, write_file, list_directory, and search_files.
The general shape of an mcp add command is:
You can configure servers at three scopes:
User scope (--scope user): available in every project. Good for personal tools (Linear, Notion).
Project scope (--scope project): committed to .mcp.json in the repo, shared with the team. Good for project-specific tools (your Supabase, your GitHub repo).
Local scope (default): only this machine, this project, your config only.

For a curated list of MCP servers worth installing (Postgres, GitHub, Playwright, Sentry, Linear, Figma, and more), see the best Claude Code MCP servers roundup. Most teams end up with 5-10 servers configured and pick which to enable per session.

A small note on security: MCP servers run with your full local permissions. Treat the mcp add command like installing a CLI tool. Only add servers from sources you trust, and read the config they write to ~/.claude.json or .mcp.json before running anything sensitive. If you want an outside review of what your team has installed and how it is configured, our Claude Code security audit checks permissions, MCP configs, and hook setups for exactly this kind of risk.
Step 6: Add a sub-agent

Sub-agents are scoped specialists you can invoke from the main session. They run with their own system prompt, their own tool allowlist, and they cannot see your main context; that is the point. Use them to parallelize, isolate risky tasks, or enforce a specific role like "code reviewer" or "test writer."
Create .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md in your repo:
That is the complete file. The frontmatter declares the agent, the body is its system prompt, and the tools field locks down what it can do (read, grep, and two specific git commands; nothing else).
In your main session, invoke it explicitly:

Or it gets invoked automatically when its description matches what you are doing. The agent runs in a fresh context, returns its report, and disappears. No token cost on your main thread for the review itself.
Common sub-agents to start with: code-reviewer, test-writer, debugger, doc-writer, migration-helper. Build the ones you actually need, not the ones from a tutorial.
Step 7: Add a hook

Hooks are shell commands the CLI runs automatically at specific lifecycle events: before a tool call, after a file edit, when the session stops, etc. They are how you wire Claude Code into your existing dev workflow without trusting the agent to remember.
The classic example is auto-format on edit. Add this to .claude/settings.json:
Now any time the agent writes a .ts or .tsx file, Prettier formats it immediately. The agent does not need to remember, you do not need to ask, and your diffs stay clean.
Other hooks worth setting up:
PreToolUse on Bash: block dangerous commands (rm -rf /, git push --force, sudo) before they run.
PostToolUse on Write: run eslint --fix on the modified file.
Stop: play a sound or send a desktop notification when the agent finishes a long task.
SessionStart: log session metadata to a file for later auditing.
Hooks are powerful and run with your shell permissions. Test them with echo "..." first before wiring up anything destructive.
Step 8: Set permissions
In .claude/settings.json:

The allow list runs without prompting. The deny list is blocked outright, even if you try to approve. The ask list always prompts. Use it for commits, installs, and other "I want to know before this happens" actions.

Tune this file as you go. A good rule: anything you'd happily watch the agent do unsupervised goes in allow. Anything you want a one-time approval prompt for goes in ask. Anything you'd fire someone for goes in deny.
Test the setup
You should now have:
claude installed and on your PATH
A working auth credential (API key, Pro, or Bedrock/Vertex)
~/.claude/settings.json with your user defaults
.claude/settings.json in your repo with project defaults + permissions + hooks
A CLAUDE.md at the repo root
At least one MCP server registered
At least one sub-agent in .claude/agents/
Smoke test it. From your repo root:
Then in the session, try:
If the agent reads the file without prompting for permission, lists the directories, and references your CLAUDE.md conventions in its answer. Your setup is wired correctly.
Try the sub-agent:
For the hook, make the agent edit a .ts file and confirm Prettier runs on it automatically:

If all three pass, you are done. Everything past this point is iteration: adding more MCP servers as you need them, growing CLAUDE.md as the agent makes mistakes, and tuning permissions as you get bolder.
MCP setup via the config file

The claude mcp add CLI command writes JSON behind the scenes. Once you understand the format, it is often faster to edit .mcp.json directly, especially when setting up a project for a team (everyone who clones the repo gets the same servers via project scope).
Create .mcp.json at your repo root:
Key fields:
type: streamable-http (or the alias http) for remote HTTP servers; omit for local stdio servers.
url: required for HTTP servers.
command + args: required for local stdio servers. Claude Code spawns the process directly.
headers: HTTP auth headers. Use ${VAR} syntax to read from the environment. Credentials stay out of version control.
timeout: per-server hard limit in milliseconds per tool call. Omit to inherit the global default.
To add a remote HTTP server without touching JSON:
Use --scope project to write to .mcp.json (committed, shared). Use --scope user to write to ~/.claude.json (personal, all projects). The default scope is local (current machine only, not committed).

After editing .mcp.json, restart Claude Code and run /mcp to confirm the servers appear as connected. Servers from .mcp.json show as "Pending approval" on first load in a freshly cloned repo until you run claude interactively and accept the workspace trust prompt.
Setup best practices
Three configuration files determine how well Claude Code works on a project long-term. Get these right and the rest follows.

CLAUDE.md (Step 4): The agent reads this at every session start. Cover your stack, the commands it can run, naming conventions, and the things you have already had to correct twice. Keep it honest: stale instructions are worse than no instructions. Most teams settle at 100-300 lines. Commit it to git.

Permissions model (.claude/settings.json, Step 8): The allow, ask, and deny lists control what the agent can do without interrupting you. Start conservative: allow for reads and lints, ask for commits and installs, deny for force-pushes and destructive commands. Widen allow as you get comfortable. A well-tuned permissions file turns a disruptive approval loop into a smooth workflow.

Hooks (.claude/settings.json hooks key, Step 7): Hooks enforce rules that you cannot rely on the model to remember: formatting on save, test runs after code changes, security checks before commits. For a curated set of hooks that cover the most common needs (linting, test automation, cost tracking, and more), see best Claude Code hooks.

The fastest path to a broken setup is treating these three files as one-time configuration and never revisiting them. CLAUDE.md rots as your stack evolves, permissions drift as you click "allow" on one-off prompts, and hooks go stale when you change your toolchain. Budget 15 minutes per sprint to review and tighten each one.
Common installation errors
A short tour of the errors most people hit in their first hour.
command not found: claude: your global npm bin is not on PATH. Run npm prefix -g to find it, then add <that path>/bin to your shell rc. Re-open the terminal.

Error: Cannot find module '@anthropic-ai/claude-code': install failed silently. Re-run with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code --verbose and check for permission errors. On macOS/Linux, prefer nvm/fnm over system Node to avoid needing sudo for global installs.

401 Unauthorized on first message: auth not set. Check echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY returns your key, or run claude auth login again (or /login inside a session). If using Bedrock/Vertex, confirm your cloud credentials work with aws sts get-caller-identity or gcloud auth list.

MCP server failed to start: usually a missing dependency for the server itself. Run the server's command manually (npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /path) and check stderr. Most MCP servers need Node 20+ even if Claude Code itself runs on Node 18.
Agent ignores CLAUDE.md: make sure the file is at the repo root, not a subdirectory, and that you launched claude from the root. The agent reads CLAUDE.md from cwd and walks up to find a git root.
Hooks not firing: JSON syntax error in .claude/settings.json. Run claude /config to validate the file, or jq . .claude/settings.json to pretty-print and catch missing commas.

Slow first response: first call after install loads the full system prompt and MCP server manifests. Subsequent calls in the same session reuse the cached prefix. If it stays slow, you have too many MCP servers enabled. Disable the ones you don't use this session with /mcp disable <name>.
If you're past these and still stuck, the official issue tracker on GitHub is well-maintained and the team responds quickly.

Setting up Claude Code well takes about thirty minutes and pays for itself in the first day. The hard part is not the install. It is keeping the configuration honest as your project grows, your team adopts the tool, and the agent's capabilities expand. That is the work that turns "I tried Claude Code" into "we ship with Claude Code." FAQ
Do I need an Anthropic API key if I have Claude Pro?

No. Claude Pro and Max subscriptions cover Claude Code usage directly. Sign in with claude auth login (or by running claude and following the browser prompts) and your sessions count against your subscription's limits instead of metered API billing. For most solo developers, Pro is the cheaper path. For a tier-by-tier breakdown of rate limits and what happens when you hit them, see Claude Code rate limits 2026.
Can I use Claude Code without Node.js?

Yes. Anthropic ships a standalone binary at claude.ai/install.sh (macOS and Linux). It is a single executable, no Node runtime required, and it is the install method Anthropic's docs recommend. The npm package installs the same binary and remains supported.
Does Claude Code work on Windows?

Yes, natively and in WSL. Anthropic's setup docs support Windows 10 1809+ and Windows Server 2019+: run irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex in PowerShell or the install.cmd command in CMD, no Administrator rights needed. Git for Windows is optional; with it, Claude Code uses Git Bash for shell commands, and without it, it uses PowerShell. Pick WSL instead if your projects and tools already live in Linux.
How much does Claude Code cost in 2026?

Two pricing models. Subscription: Pro at $20/month ($17/month billed annually) or Max from $100/month, per claude.com/pricing in October 2026. API: metered per token. Heavy users typically spend $50-500/month depending on model choice and prompt size. Bedrock/Vertex bills through your cloud account at similar rates. Switch with /model to control cost mid-session.
What is the difference between CLAUDE.md and a system prompt?

CLAUDE.md is project memory: it loads at every session start from your repo and stays in context. A system prompt is set once at the API level and applies to all conversations. For Claude Code specifically, you write CLAUDE.md, you do not write a system prompt. The CLI handles the system prompt for you.
Should I commit .claude/ to git?

Yes for settings.json, agents/, and any project-level MCP config. No for transient files (sessions, caches). Those go in .gitignore. Sharing .claude/ is how your team gets the same defaults, sub-agents, and hooks without each developer setting it up manually.
Can I run multiple Claude Code sessions at once?

Yes. Each terminal window is an independent session. Sub-agents run in their own context inside a session. Many teams run two or three sessions in parallel: one for the main feature, one for tests, one for docs. Tile them in your terminal multiplexer.
How do I update Claude Code?

Run claude update, or npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@latest for an npm install (the docs advise against npm update -g). Anthropic ships updates roughly weekly in 2026. The CLI will tell you on launch if there is a new version. Native installs auto-update in the background by default (Homebrew and WinGet installs do not). To turn the background updater off for version-pinned environments, set "DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER": "1" in the env block of settings.json; DISABLE_UPDATES also blocks manual updates.
